status_label: China truce runs to Jan 10, 2027. Soybeans still pay the extra 10%.
status_note:
What applies today: US soybeans into China face about 13% (3% MFN plus China's broad 10% retaliatory levy); corn and wheat about 11%, pork about 22%. On Sep 28, 2026, after the Trump-Xi summit in Washington, the two governments published matching tariff-cut lists on about $60B of two-way trade. China's list trims duties on US corn, wheat, sorghum, meat, dairy, vegetable oils and meals; soybeans are not on it. No timing or size was given. The July 6 report that the 10% would go for all US farm goods arriving after Oct 1 did not come true for soybeans.

The Busan truce, due to end Nov 10, was extended to Jan 10, 2027 (Bessent, Sep 24; China's commerce ministry confirmed Sep 29). China's purchase commitment is 25 MMT of soybeans a year for 2026-2028. About 13.7 MMT was bought before Chinese state firms booked 8 to 10 more cargoes the week of Oct 12 (Reuters, Oct 14).

Tariff authority: the Supreme Court voided the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. The Section 122 surcharge that replaced them was ruled invalid by the Court of International Trade on May 7, 2026 (under appeal) and ran out around Jul 24. Section 301 'forced labor' duties took effect Jul 24, 2026 at 10-12.5% on 60 trading partners and about 99.4% of US imports. Fertilizer, pesticides, in-quota sugar and certain planting seeds are exempt.

Canada: counter-tariffs took effect Sep 8, 2026 on C$27.6B of US goods at 15%, 25% and 50% (steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, electronics; natural honey is on the list). Bulk grain, oilseeds, fertilizer and seeds are not, so the 0% rows are unchanged. The US answered with five Section 338 proclamations: import bans on certain Canadian alcohol and dairy since Sep 29, and list changes effective Sep 15. This is running alongside a USMCA renegotiation, and August's 50% Section 338 duties already overrode USMCA origin once.

Brazil: a 25% tariff on Brazilian goods including ethanol landed mid-July after a Section 301 investigation. That helps US corn ethanol at home.

Check USTR, the Federal Register and Canada's Department of Finance before any trading decision.
headline: China's Sep 28 tariff-cut list covers US corn, wheat, sorghum, meat and dairy but not soybeans, which still face about 13%. China has not said when the cuts start or how big they are, so the corn, wheat and pork rates below stand until it does. State buyers took 8 to 10 US soybean cargoes this week, the first since the summit, for December shipment (Reuters, Oct 14). Canada's counter-tariffs (Sep 8) and the US bans on some Canadian alcohol and dairy (Sep 29) do not touch grain, oilseeds, fertilizer or seed.

rows.note: China lifted its March 2025 retaliatory 10% on soybeans under the Busan agreement (effective Nov 10, 2025) but kept its broad 10% 'Liberation Day' levy, so US soybeans face about 13% (3% MFN + 10%), a lasting edge for Brazil. Soybeans were left off China's Sep 28 tariff-cut list, so the 10% stays. State buyers still booked 8 to 10 cargoes the week of Oct 12 (Reuters). The truce runs to Jan 10, 2027.

China suspended its March 2025 retaliatory 15% on corn under the Busan agreement but kept the broad 10% levy, leaving about 11% (1% MFN + 10%). China's Sep 28 list trims duties on US corn but gave no date or size, so this rate stands until China's tariff commission publishes the cut. China has bought little US corn since the levy dropped. The truce runs to Jan 10, 2027.

March 2025 retaliatory 15% suspended under the Busan agreement; the broad 10% levy remains (about 11% = 1% MFN + 10%). China's Sep 28 list trims duties on US wheat but gave no date or size, so this rate stands until China publishes the cut. US wheat sells little to China directly; world trade flows matter more than this rate.

March 2025 retaliatory 10% suspended under the Busan agreement; the broad 10% levy remains (about 22% = 12% MFN + 10%). China resumed US beef and poultry access under the May 18, 2026 deal. China's Sep 28 list trims duties on US meat (pork is not named separately in the reports) but gave no date or size, so this rate stands until China publishes the cut.

USMCA, duty-free. The USMCA renegotiation opened July 2026; rates are unchanged so far. In August, 50% Section 338 duties hit Canadian dairy, alcohol and vehicles even with USMCA origin. Canada's C$27.6B counter-tariffs (Sep 8) leave out bulk grain, oilseeds, fertilizer and seeds, checked against Canada's own published list, so this rate is unchanged.

USMCA, duty-free. Mexico is still the top US corn buyer. The USMCA renegotiation opened July 2026; rates are unchanged so far. In August, 50% Section 338 duties hit Canadian dairy, alcohol and vehicles even with USMCA origin. Canada's C$27.6B counter-tariffs (Sep 8) leave out bulk grain, oilseeds, fertilizer and seeds, checked against Canada's own published list, so this rate is unchanged.

No EU anti-dumping duty on US ethanol. The 2013 duty was repealed by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/765, in force May 16, 2019. What remains is the ordinary EU import duty: €192/m³ undenatured, €102/m³ denatured, the same in every member state. The Dutch RED III vote of Oct 2025 bars imported denatured ethanol from counting toward renewable-fuel obligations from 2026; that is a compliance rule, not a duty. The UK-US deal (May 2025) opened a 1.4B L/yr duty-free quota for the UK only.

timeline.event: Chinese state firms buy 8 to 10 US soybean cargoes for December shipment, the first deals since the Trump-Xi summit, trade sources tell Reuters. China had bought about 13.7 MMT toward its 25 MMT commitment before these. Private crushers are still mostly out because of the 10% levy.

US import bans on certain Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles over 800cc take effect under Section 338, replacing the 50% duty on those lines. Goods already imported but not entered before Sep 29 stay at 50%.

After the Trump-Xi summit, the US and China publish matching tariff-cut lists on about $60B of two-way trade. China's covers US corn, wheat, sorghum, meat, dairy, vegetable oils and meals; soybeans are excluded and keep the extra 10%. No timing or size given. The truce is extended to Jan 10, 2027.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the Busan truce, due to end Nov 10, will be extended to Jan 10, 2027. US soybeans into China are still at 13% (10% retaliatory + 3% MFN) as Trump and Xi meet Sep 24-25.
China is roughly halfway through its 25 MMT 2026 soybean commitment after buying about 1 MMT in a week. The 10% levy still makes US beans less attractive to private Chinese crushers.

The President signs five Section 338 proclamations in response to Canada: import bans on certain Canadian alcohol and dairy effective Sep 29, 2026, plus list changes effective Sep 15 removing rock salt and cement and adding all-terrain vehicles and further dairy products.

Canada's counter-tariffs take effect: C$27.6B of US imports at 15%, 25% and 50% across steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics. Bulk grain, oilseeds, fertilizer and seeds are not on the published list.

Canada announces counter-tariffs on C$27.6B of US imports, effective Sep 8: 50% on steel and aluminum, furniture, clothing and some dairy; 25% on appliances, some dairy (including cheese) and paper; 15% on select tools, handling machinery and agricultural equipment. Natural honey is on the list. No bulk grain or oilseed is named.

US imposes 50% Section 338 duties on roughly $20B of Canadian imports: dairy (notably TRQ cheese), alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles, plus a longer covered list that reaches honey, certain planting seeds, molasses and fructose syrups. Grain and oilseeds are not covered. The date differs by source: counsel reported it effective Aug 19, customs brokers put it at 12:01 a.m. ET Aug 22 for entries on or after that date; confirm the entry date for a specific shipment. USMCA origin does not exempt covered goods, which is the first time duty-free USMCA treatment has been overridden outright while the agreement is being renegotiated.

China is roughly a quarter of the way through its 25 MMT/yr soybean commitment for 2026, behind pace with a Trump-Xi meeting expected in September. Buying accelerated into that meeting; private crushers reportedly held back.

Section 301 'forced labor' duties take effect at 10-12.5% across 60 trading partners, covering about 99.4% of US imports and replacing the lapsed Section 122 surcharge (goods in transit had a grace period to July 28). Agricultural exemptions apply universally to in-quota sugar, fertilizer and pesticides, and certain planting seeds, so input costs are shielded. Five economies were cut to 10% after forced-labour import bans or trade commitments; the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan get a modified MFN-ceiling method where existing duties count toward the cap instead of stacking on top.

USMCA bilateral negotiations resume in Mexico City, the first talks since the Administration signaled it would not renew the agreement. No ag rate changes announced; Canada/Mexico access (top two US ag export destinations) rides on the outcome.

25% tariff on Brazilian goods, including ethanol, announced the prior week following a Section 301 investigation. Inbound tariff: Brazilian ethanol had been gaining US market share, so this helps US corn ethanol's domestic position.

Reported deal to unwind the last ag levy: China would drop its 10% tax on US agricultural goods for cargoes arriving after October 1, timed to when China normally shifts from Brazilian to US supply. The report says the US side would end its 10% fentanyl tariff, though the Supreme Court had already voided the IEEPA fentanyl tariffs on Feb 20, so what the US would give up is unclear. China's Ministry of Commerce confirmed the agreement; USTR had not confirmed it at the time of reporting. This is the levy that keeps US soybeans near 13%. It had not come off by the Sep 24 and Sep 28 entries above: soybeans were still at 13% and left off China's tariff-cut list.

The Administration signals it will not renew USMCA and will instead open new negotiations. House Ag Democrats and ag groups flag the risk: tariff-free access hits corn, beef, pork, and dairy before anything else.

USTR proposes Section 301 'forced labor' tariffs of 10-12.5% on 59 countries and the EU, with some agricultural exemptions (Annex A). Public comment runs to July 6, hearing July 7, timed to maintain duties after the Section 122 surcharge expires around July 24.

US-China deal during President Trump's state visit: China to buy at least $17B/yr in US agricultural products through 2028 (in addition to the Oct 2025 soybean commitments) and resumes purchases of US beef and poultry.

US Court of International Trade rules the Section 122 global 10% surcharge (Proclamation 11012) invalid for failing to identify the required balance-of-payments deficit (Oregon v. United States; Burlap & Barrel v. United States). The ruling is under appeal and does not automatically halt collections.

Section 122 global tariff takes effect at 10% (administration announced intent to raise to 15%) after the IEEPA tariffs were terminated. The 150-day statutory clock runs to roughly July 24, 2026 unless Congress extends it.

US Supreme Court rules 6-3 in Learning Resources v. Trump that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs; the April 2025 reciprocal and fentanyl tariffs are voided. The administration pivots to Section 122 the same day.
China lifts the up-to-15% retaliatory ag tariffs from its March 2025 tranche under the Busan agreement, but keeps the broad 10% 'Liberation Day' retaliatory levy, leaving US soybeans at roughly 13%.

Trump-Xi meeting in Busan, South Korea: tariff truce reached. China commits to buy 12 MMT of US soybeans in late 2025 and 25 MMT/yr in 2026-2028; the truce is set to run one year, to Nov 10, 2026, and is later extended to Jan 10, 2027.

China announces first-tranche retaliatory tariffs on US ag, effective Mar 10, 2025 (15% on wheat, corn, cotton, chicken; 10% on soybeans, pork, beef, dairy), later suspended under the Oct 30, 2025 Busan agreement.
